Fleet and Device-Lifetime Metrics

What a device earns and costs over its life in the field — and why the answer changes every month it stays installed.

1. A cohort that will not sit still

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Maya Krishnan, VP of Product at Tarquin Systems, a Pune-based company that retrofits diesel generators at small factories with a connectivity kit and sells the resulting uptime data as a subscription, opened the board pre-read three days before the Series C renewal discussion. The pre-read asked one question the deck did not answer cleanly: was the fleet of 10,000 units shipped in the first quarter of 2024 making money yet, eighteen months in? Tarquin's investors had underwritten the company on a simple story — sell the hardware near cost, recover the margin over 24 to 36 months of subscription revenue from each connected device. Whether that story was true depended entirely on how many of those 10,000 boxes were still bolted to a generator, still transmitting, and still being billed.

Maya had two spreadsheets that disagreed. Finance measured "installed base" as everything ever shipped minus everything ever returned: 9,412 units, a healthy-looking number implying the fleet was nearly intact. Field operations measured "active fleet" as devices that had pinged telemetry in the last 30 days: 7,150 units, 24% lower. Neither number, alone, told Maya whether Tarquin's hardware economics worked. She needed to see the whole life of a device — from the day it shipped to the day it paid for itself or didn't — with arithmetic the board could check, not a felt sense that things were "mostly fine."

2. The idea

Fleet and device-lifetime metrics are the set of measures that track a population of physical, connected units through the stages of their working life — shipped, activated, connected and paying, failed or disconnected, replaced — and attach a cost or a revenue figure to each stage, so hardware economics can be judged the way software economics are judged: per cohort, over time, against what it cost to create that cohort. The discipline has no single inventor or founding paper; it is an assembly of three older traditions that connected hardware forced together after roughly 2015: reliability engineering (mean time between failures, hazard curves, a lineage running back to Bell Labs and military aerospace in the 1950s), automotive and industrial fleet telematics (odometer- and sensor-based maintenance tracking, matured through the 1990s and 2000s), and SaaS cohort-retention analysis (the practice, popularized through the 2000s and 2010s by growth and venture practitioners such as David Skok, of tracking a signup cohort's survival and revenue month by month rather than a single blended snapshot). When companies began selling connected hardware as a subscription — fitness trackers, POS terminals, industrial sensors, retrofit kits like Tarquin's — they needed the SaaS habit of cohort thinking applied to something that could also physically break, get stolen, or sit powered off in a warehouse. That combination is what this topic names.

The sentence Maya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this:

"A device only earns what it stays alive, installed and connected long enough to earn — so the question is never 'how many did we ship,' it's 'how many field-months of paying connection did this cohort actually produce, against what it cost us to put them in the field.'"

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in five stages, and the step practitioners most often skip is insisting each stage have its own denominator rather than reusing "units shipped" for everything. First, activation: the fraction of shipped devices physically installed and registered with the backend, measured within a fixed window (Tarquin uses 30 days). Second, connected usage: of the activated base, the fraction still sending telemetry within a trailing window — typically 30 days — at any later date; this is the metric field operations was using, and it is a moving target, always read as "connected as of month N," never as a static number. Third, failure: devices confirmed dead through a service ticket, warranty claim, or diagnostic flag, expressed as a hazard rate against the activated base at each month of fleet age, not against total shipments. Fourth, replacement and attrition: what happens to a failed or disconnected unit — swapped under warranty (a cost), left dark (a write-off and data gap), or voluntarily removed by the customer (churn, not failure). Fifth, and the step most teams skip, field-economics attribution: multiplying each month a device stays connected by its monthly contribution margin, summing across its actual life, and comparing that sum to build, ship and install cost. Skipping this last step is how a company ends up with a healthy activation rate and a fleet quietly losing money on every unit.

Figure 1. The five-stage funnel for one cohort. Finance's "installed base" (9,412 = shipped minus confirmed returns) sat between Activated and Connected, and hid the 910 dark units entirely.

4. A worked example, line by line

Each Tarquin unit costs ₹6,500 in bill of materials plus ₹2,500 in logistics and technician installation, a fully loaded build-and-install cost of ₹9,000. The subscription is ₹899 per connected unit per month, and finance holds gross margin on that revenue at 70%, or ₹629 of contribution per connected device-month. The question is how many device-months of connection the Q1 2024 cohort produced by month 18, and whether that covered the ₹9,000 build cost.

Of the 10,000 shipped, 8,700 activated within 30 days (87%; the other 1,300 never registered — ₹1.17 crore of build cost that never had a chance to earn). Connection did not hold at 100% from day one: it starts near full strength just after activation and drifts down as units fail or go dark, reaching 82.2% of the activated base (7,150 of 8,700) by month 18. Averaged across the 18 months, the connected fraction works out to roughly 78% — call it 14 device-months of paying connection per activated unit (0.78 × 18). At ₹629 per device-month, that is ₹8,806 of contribution earned per activated device by month 18.

Against that, 640 of the 8,700 activated units (7.4%) were confirmed hardware failures requiring a ₹4,200 warranty replacement each — ₹26.88 lakh total, or ₹309 spread across every activated device. Net contribution per activated device at month 18: ₹8,806 minus ₹309, or ₹8,497 — short of the ₹9,000 build-and-install cost. Table 1 shows the arithmetic, and a second pass shows what changes when one input moves.

InputGen1 (shipped Q1 2024)Gen2 (revised firmware)
Activated, of 10,000 shipped8,700 (87%)8,700 (87%)
Connected at month 18, % of activated82.2%91.0%
Avg. connected device-months (of 18)≈14.0≈16.9

The one input Maya changed for the second pass was the firmware revision Tarquin pushed to devices manufactured after month 9, which fixed a class of sensor-drift failures customers had misread as "the box stopped working," prompting them to switch it off rather than call for service. Connection held closer to 100% for longer, the true failure rate fell, and the same cohort economics that looked underwater at month 18 turned solidly profitable. The lesson in the two columns: fleet economics are not a fixed property of the business model; they are a function of engineering decisions that surface months later in a metric most executives check only once a quarter.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Activation, registration and shipment are three different denominators

Teams routinely report "fleet size" using whichever of the three makes the headline number largest. A rigorous metrics tree names all three and never lets one stand in for another on a board slide.

"Connected" is not the same as "alive and working"

A device can be powered on and functioning correctly, simply sitting in a connectivity dead zone, producing a false churn signal identical to a real failure until someone visits the site.

Failure and voluntary churn are different events with different costs

A hardware failure triggers a warranty replacement cost; a customer unplugging and cancelling triggers a lost-revenue event but no replacement cost. Blending them into one "attrition rate" hides which lever — reliability or customer value — actually needs fixing.

Survivorship bias creeps into every average

Average field life calculated only from devices still reporting will overstate true fleet health, because units most likely to have failed have already stopped contributing data to the average.

Warranty life, field life and economic life are three different clocks

A device can be within its 24-month warranty, still functioning at month 40, yet economically obsolete the day a cheaper Gen3 unit ships — three separate expirations a single "device lifetime" number quietly conflates.

Cohort and vintage effects hide inside fleet-wide averages

A single blended failure rate across all shipments obscures that one manufacturing batch, firmware version, or dusty geography is doing most of the damage; only a cohort-cut survival curve, sliced by ship month, exposes it.

A "dark" device is not the same liability as a confirmed failure

An unreturned, unaccounted-for unit carries write-off and grey-market resale risk and an unresolved data gap that a confirmed, returned failure does not; treating the two identically in a warranty reserve misstates the true exposure.

The metric cannot tell you why, only how much

Fleet metrics tell Maya precisely how many device-months of connection a cohort produced; they will not tell her, unassisted, whether a spike in one district was a monsoon outage, a rival unplugging boxes, or a software bug — that needs a root-cause investigation the metric only flags.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace hardware look different

In consumer connected hardware — a fitness band or a home water purifier — volumes are large, revenue per device is small, installation is self-service, and activation itself is the most fragile stage of the funnel; a large share of shipped units never register, and disconnection afterward is usually silent, with no support call and no clean signal of cause. In B2B fleets like Tarquin's, a technician performs the install, volumes are smaller, revenue per device is much higher, and downtime typically sits inside a service-level agreement, which turns a replacement decision from a cost-center question into a contractual liability with penalty clauses attached. In marketplace-supplied hardware — a payments terminal a platform hands a small merchant at a subsidy — "activation" is better measured by transaction volume than registration, and the sharpest risk is a merchant leaving the platform while still holding the device, which turns fleet metrics into a channel-risk and subsidy-allocation question as much as a hardware-economics one. Stage matters as much as model: an early-stage team with a few hundred units can review fleet health by eyeballing a spreadsheet, founder or PM as de facto owner; once a fleet reaches Tarquin's 10,000-unit scale, the discipline must formalize into an owned metrics tree with a named cadence, automated cohort dashboards, and a reliability-engineering function feeding failure data into the next hardware revision.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting activated units as if they were the whole revenue base. Symptom: a subscription-revenue forecast that consistently misses low. Underlying error: the forecast multiplies price by "installed base" instead of the connected-and-billing fraction, silently assuming every activated unit pays every month. Cheapest diagnostic: reconcile shipped, activated and currently-billing counts monthly, and ask finance which one fed the forecast.

Averaging failure rate across every vintage at once. Symptom: a maintenance and warranty budget wrong in both directions — too generous for healthy cohorts, too thin for a bad batch. Underlying error: treating the fleet as one population instead of cohorts with different manufacturing dates and firmware. Cheapest diagnostic: cut the survival curve by ship-month and firmware version before setting any budget.

Counting every disconnection as a failure for warranty accounting. Symptom: a warranty reserve that balloons even though field visits find most "dead" units merely powered off. Underlying error: no distinction between confirmed failure and unexplained silence. Cheapest diagnostic: run a sample outbound campaign — an SMS ping or a field visit to a random slice of dark devices — and see how many are actually broken.

Leaving the metric without a named owner, cadence or decision. Symptom: fleet health gets discussed only when a board deck forces the question, as it did for Maya. Underlying error: nobody's role is defined as owning the number between board meetings. Cheapest diagnostic: ask who reviews the cohort dashboard weekly and what decision changes if it moves — if no one can answer, the metric has no owner.

Figure 2. The survival curve, not the month-18 snapshot alone, is what should govern the breakeven calculation — the area under each curve is the device-months of connection actually earned.

8. What good looks like

Six months after that board pre-read, Rohan Desai, who runs field operations at Sahayak Tools, a competitor of Tarquin's fitting sensors to borewell pumps across three states, walked his own board through a cohort dashboard that updated automatically every Monday: shipped, activated, connected, confirmed-failed and dark, each tracked separately by ship-month and firmware version, each with a named owner and a monthly review cadence written into the operating rhythm rather than assembled under deadline. When a March 2025 cohort showed connection dropping faster than any prior vintage, the dashboard flagged it within three weeks, not eighteen months; a targeted field-visit sample found a batch of SIM cards provisioned with the wrong data plan, fixed within a billing cycle rather than discovered at a fundraising review. Good fleet-metrics practice is not a more sophisticated spreadsheet; it is a standing habit of asking, cohort by cohort and month by month, whether the field is still earning what it cost to put there.

9. What Maya decided

Maya told the board the truth in two sentences: the Gen1 cohort had not yet broken even at month 18, but the Gen2 firmware fix showed a clear, arithmetic path to profitability for every cohort shipped after month 9, and the company's job now was to retrofit that fix to the field wherever possible rather than wait for natural replacement. The board approved a technician-led firmware campaign instead of a defensive write-down. The reasoning was not optimism; it was that the cohort table made the mechanism of the problem, and the mechanism of the fix, equally visible and equally measurable. Maya's next step was to build the same cohort-and-survival discipline into how Tarquin evaluates a whole portfolio of hardware products, which is where fleet metrics connect to lifetime-value modelling across a multi-product line. Two questions worth sitting with: when your own dashboard shows a healthy "installed base," have you checked what fraction of that base is actually connected and paying this month, not merely shipped? And when a device goes quiet, do you know — with evidence, not assumption — whether it broke, or whether someone simply turned it off?

Sheetkosh Coldchain: What Is a Freezer Worth?

Ahmedabad, August 2026. Nine thousand deep freezers are coming to the end of their deployment term, and nobody at Sheetkosh can agree on what any one of them has actually earned.

1. The decision

On the morning of 7 August 2026, Devika Shenoy walked past the loading bay of Sheetkosh Coldchain Systems' refurbishment yard in Naroda, on the eastern edge of Ahmedabad, and counted freezers. There were four hundred of them in rows, pulled out of kirana stores and dairy parlours across Gujarat and Maharashtra, waiting for a decision she had to make by 22 August. Navratri began on 11 October, and the festive deployment wave — the busiest eight weeks of Sheetkosh's year — had to be locked by the end of August for the fleet team in Pune to plan trucks.

Devika had been Head of Product for two years. The decision in front of her was, on paper, a procurement question: 9,240 connected deep freezers deployed in FY21 and FY22 were reaching the end of their five-year contracted term. Sheetkosh could refurbish and redeploy them, replace them with a new energy-efficient model, or do something else entirely. On the finance team's model the answer was obvious and cheap. On the operations team's model it was obvious and expensive. Both models were built from the same database.

2. The company

Sheetkosh did not sell freezers. It ran cooling as a service. A frozen-foods or ice-cream brand contracted with Sheetkosh to place a branded deep freezer in a retail outlet, and paid Sheetkosh a monthly fee — ₹1,450 for the standard 300-litre hard-top unit — covering the freezer, the telemetry, the service and the eventual removal. The retailer paid nothing and kept the electricity bill. Sheetkosh owned the asset, and every freezer carried a controller that reported cabinet temperature, door openings, compressor run time and power state over a cellular link.

The company had been founded in 2018 by two former cold-chain managers who had watched brands lose crores to freezers that were placed and then forgotten. By 2026 it operated 61,400 units across eleven states, working with regional ice-cream brands, frozen-snack companies and two national players, in a market where Amul's own deep-freezer network set the standard every retailer compared against. Reliance Retail and the quick-commerce platforms — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — had changed the shape of demand: frozen impulse purchase was migrating from the kirana counter to a ten-minute delivery, and brands were asking harder questions about what a store-level freezer still earned.

Sheetkosh had a second business. The fleet dashboard it had built for itself was licensed as software to cold-chain operators abroad: a distributor in Dubai ran 3,100 units on it, and Brian Kowalski, the sales head in New Jersey, had two American ice-cream distributors in late-stage discussions. That business was small — about ₹9 crore of annual revenue — but it carried 78% gross margin and it was the reason the board tolerated Sheetkosh's engineering headcount in Bengaluru and Pune.

3. The situation

The trouble had started in June, when Ananya Bhattacharya, Sheetkosh's data scientist in Toronto, rebuilt the fleet report for the software product and found that the company's two internal numbers for freezer life did not agree. Finance's model assumed a seven-year useful life and depreciated accordingly; its per-unit economics looked comfortable. Operations in Pune worked from service history and put median life at closer to five and a half years, with compressor replacement the dominant failure after year four. Neither number was wrong. They measured different things — finance measured how long a freezer could exist, operations measured how long it stayed in service.

Ananya's rebuild surfaced a third number that neither team tracked. Since the telemetry upgrade in 2023, every unit reported cold hours: hours in which the cabinet held below −18 °C with the compressor powered. Across the FY21–22 cohorts, the median unit delivered 6,340 cold hours a year against a theoretical 8,760. The gap was not failure. It was retailers switching freezers off overnight to save electricity, which they paid for themselves. In the lowest tercile of outlets, cold hours fell to 4,100 — the freezer was off for more than half the year, the brand's stock was repeatedly thawed and refrozen, and the brand's area manager logged the resulting complaints as Sheetkosh service failures.

Sameer Gokhale, who led engineering from Bengaluru, pointed out the second-order consequence on a call at 7 a.m. India time so that Ananya could join from Toronto the previous evening. Every power cycle is a compressor start, and compressor starts, not running hours, drive wear. The units in the worst outlets were both earning least and dying fastest. "We have been replacing compressors," he said, "in exactly the freezers that should never have been placed there."

Adeline Yeo, the customer-success lead in Singapore who handled the Dubai distributor, raised a different worry. The distributor had begun using the cold-hours metric in its own conversations with retailers and wanted it exposed through the API. If Sheetkosh changed how cold hours were computed as part of this decision, a paying software customer's dashboards would move. Brian Kowalski, in New Jersey, had been quoting the same metric to American prospects as evidence that Sheetkosh's fleet data was audit-grade.

4. The people

Devika Shenoy, Head of Product, Ahmedabad, owns the decision. She wants a rule the company can apply every year to every expiring cohort, not a one-off answer for this one. Parth Trivedi, Chief Financial Officer, Ahmedabad, has ₹18 crore of approved capex for FY27 and a Series C conversation opening in January; he wants the fleet to grow without consuming it. Raghav Pillai, VP Operations, Pune, runs 340 field technicians and a refurbishment yard; his team's overtime has risen 22% in a year, almost all of it on units older than four years, and he wants the FY21–22 cohorts replaced outright. Ananya Bhattacharya, data scientist, Toronto, owns the survival model and keeps repeating an uncomfortable caveat: the cold-hours series only begins in 2023, so for the FY21 cohort the company has no idea what the first two years looked like.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. FY21–22 cohorts at 30 June 2026: state and cold-hours by outlet tercile

Exhibit 1 is the heart of the case. The three terciles are not three grades of freezer — they are the same freezer in three kinds of outlet. The bottom third delivers half the cooling, survives least, and consumes nearly five times the compressor work of the top third. Any conclusion that treats the cohort as a single population will be an average of these three, and will describe none of them.

Exhibit 2. Five-year economics per freezer, by tercile (₹, undiscounted)

Freezer cost ₹38,400 landed. Residual value is the yard's assessed refurbishment value at removal and is lower for bottom-tercile units because of compressor and gasket wear. Brand fee is billed monthly and credited against a service-level clause when a unit is out of temperature for more than 48 hours in a month.

Exhibit 2 converts the physics of Exhibit 1 into money. The top third returns ₹41,300 over five years; the bottom third loses ₹24,100. Across the cohort the average is a modest ₹14,000 per unit, which is roughly the number Parth's model reported and the reason nobody had treated this as urgent. The average conceals a third of the fleet that destroys value in every line of the table simultaneously — less revenue, more credits, more service, worse residual.

6. The options

Option A — refurbish and redeploy all 9,240 units. The yard can recondition a unit for about ₹6,200 and return it to service for a further three years. Capex is minimal, about ₹5.7 crore, and Parth's model likes it. The cost is that Sheetkosh would redeploy roughly three thousand units into outlets where they have already lost money, with compressors that have done four years of hard cycling, and Raghav's technicians would carry the consequences through the festive season.

Option B — replace all 9,240 with the new 5-star model. The new unit costs ₹44,800 landed, draws 31% less power, and carries a controller with per-hour reporting rather than per-six-hours. Total capex is ₹41.4 crore against ₹18 crore approved, so it would need either a lease facility or a cut elsewhere. It solves the service-load problem and gives Adeline and Brian a better data product to sell, but it spends the most money on exactly the question the data says is not primarily about the hardware.

Option C — re-place rather than replace. Withdraw from the bottom tercile of outlets, refurbish the withdrawn units, and redeploy them into the placement queue of high-cold-hour outlets that Sheetkosh's sales team already has, buying only enough new units to cover the shortfall. Capex falls to roughly ₹11 crore. The costs are commercial and human: brands lose 3,000 points of presence at the start of a festive quarter, four brand relationships would have to be renegotiated, and Sheetkosh would have to tell retailers who have had a freezer for five years that it is being taken away during Navratri.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Finance says the median freezer lives seven years; operations says five and a half. What exactly is each measuring, and which of the two belongs in a decision about redeployment?

2. Ananya has cold-hours data only from March 2023. What does that do to the reliability of Exhibit 2, and what would you do about it before 22 August?

3. Exhibit 3 shows that contribution tracks the outlet, not the device. What follows for how Sheetkosh should price its service to brands?

4. Which option would you take to the board on 22 August, and what would you commit to measure by the same date next year?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about what happens when a company measures devices by calendar time instead of by earning time. Sheetkosh had two lifetime numbers, both honest, and neither of them was the one that mattered, because both asked how long a freezer survives rather than how many hours it spent doing the thing it is paid for. Once cold hours enter the model, the fleet stops being one population of 9,240 assets and becomes three populations with contributions that differ by ₹65,000 per unit.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It separates the question of what to do with the asset from the question of where the asset should sit, because the data says the second matters more. It treats the bottom tercile as a placement failure to be corrected rather than a hardware failure to be re-bought. And it is explicit about the weakness in the evidence: the FY21 cohort's first two years are unobserved, terciles are defined on FY25 behaviour, and an outlet that has improved is being judged on its past — so any withdrawal list should be re-scored on the most recent twelve months before a truck is sent.

One defensible path is a staged version of Option C. Re-score every FY21–22 unit on trailing-twelve-month cold hours rather than the FY25 tercile. Withdraw only the worst decile immediately — roughly 900 units whose economics are unambiguous — and refurbish them for the placement queue. Put the remaining bottom-tercile outlets on a ninety-day improvement offer: Sheetkosh funds a timer and a power-factor fix, the retailer commits to continuous operation, and the freezer stays. Buy about 2,000 new 5-star units for the festive wave, well inside Parth's ₹18 crore. Then change the thing that actually caused the problem: bill brands on a cold-hours band rather than a flat ₹1,450, so that Sheetkosh, the brand and the retailer are all paid for the same thing. The argument to the board is that the company is not choosing between refurbishing and replacing; it is choosing to stop treating a placement decision as a procurement decision, and it now has the fleet data to make that stick.

Tejomay Energy Networks: The Night Before the Board

Bengaluru, Sunday 20 September 2026. Forty-one thousand battery packs are circulating through Tejomay's swap network, and the company has at least four different numbers for how long one of them lasts.

1. Sunday night

The office on the third floor above a bakery in Koramangala was empty except for Kartik Bhandari and the hum of a test cabinet in the corner, which had been swapping the same four packs in and out of a rig since March. It was a quarter past ten. The board pack was due to the directors at seven the next morning, and the slide that mattered — slide 11, titled "Pratidin: recommendation" — still had a placeholder on it.

Pratidin Logistics, a last-mile fleet running about 14,000 electric two-wheelers for quick-commerce and pharmacy deliveries across six cities, had put a three-year energy contract out to tender. The volume was enormous by Tejomay's standards: a commitment of 41 lakh swaps a year, roughly 63% of the network's current throughput, at a price Pratidin had already anchored at ₹58 a swap against Tejomay's list price of ₹74. Winning it would fill stations that ran at 34% utilisation. Losing it would hand a competitor the density that made the network defensible.

Kartik had spent three weeks trying to answer one question and had failed. If a pack does 2.3 swaps a day and Pratidin's riders arrive with the pack at a lower state of charge than everyone else, how many rupees of battery does each swap consume? Everything — the price, the reserve, the capital plan, the story to the board — depended on that number, and the company had produced it four times with four different answers.

2. How Tejomay got here, and the decision that still binds it

Tejomay Energy Networks was founded in Bengaluru in 2021 by Sunaina Kamath and two engineers from a power-electronics background. The idea was simple and, in 2021, unfashionable: instead of selling electric scooters, sell the energy. Tejomay built cabinets — ventilated steel towers of eight slots each — and placed them at fuel stations, kirana clusters and parking lots. A rider pulled out a depleted pack, slid in a charged one, and paid per swap through UPI. By September 2026 there were 1,180 cabinets across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Delhi NCR, 41,300 packs in circulation, and about 65 lakh swaps a year.

The decision that still bound the company had been taken in October 2022. Tejomay had to choose a cell chemistry. Lithium iron phosphate — LFP — was cheaper per kWh, tolerated heat better and lasted more cycles, but was heavier for the same energy. Nickel-manganese-cobalt — NMC — was lighter, and weight mattered because a rider had to lift the pack out of a scooter and into a slot at chest height, sometimes forty times a shift for a fleet rider. Sunaina chose NMC, and the company then did the thing that made the choice irreversible: it designed the cabinet, the slot geometry, the thermal duct and the connector around that specific pack. Switching chemistry now meant re-engineering the cabinet, not just the pack.

The supplier, a Gujarat-based pack assembler working with imported cells, warranted 1,800 cycles to 80% state of health under standard conditions — 25 °C ambient, 1C charge, full depth of discharge. That number went into Tejomay's first financial model in 2022 and, four years later, it had never come out.

3. The industry around it

India's electric two-wheeler market had matured fast. Ather Energy and Ola Electric had built large fixed-battery installed bases with home and fast charging; Hero and Bajaj had entered at scale; TVS was pushing into fleet segments. Swapping had grown alongside as a separate architecture, aimed squarely at riders for whom downtime is income — the gig riders delivering for Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto and Blinkit, and the three-wheeler operators moving goods in Delhi and Hyderabad. Sun Mobility, Battery Smart and Honda's power-pack venture had all built networks; each had made its own bet on chemistry, form factor and who owns the battery.

Policy had been generous but unstable in its details. Central incentives had moved from FAME II to a successor scheme with different eligibility for swapping infrastructure; state EV policies in Delhi and Maharashtra treated swap stations differently from charging points; NITI Aayog's battery-swapping consultations had raised, and then left unresolved, the question of interoperability standards. The Battery Waste Management Rules put an extended producer responsibility obligation on Tejomay for every pack it put into circulation, with a documented end-of-life route. GST treatment — batteries taxed differently from the vehicles they power — was a live grievance across the industry, and it mattered to Tejomay because the company, not the rider, owned the asset.

Tejomay's exposure was not only Indian. Charmaine Koh, the customer-success lead in Singapore, ran a pilot with Barq Mobility, a Dubai last-mile operator with 600 scooters. Dev Mathur, the sales head in New Jersey, had a pipeline of American micromobility operators who wanted to license Tejomay's cabinet design and fleet software rather than the packs themselves. Both needed a published cycle-life figure. Both had been given 1,800.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence mattered, and Kartik had written it out on the whiteboard behind him in the order in which the company had believed things.

In 2022 and 2023, with a small fleet and mostly retail riders, packs behaved close to the supplier's curve. Average utilisation was 1.1 swaps per pack per day, riders typically arrived with 20–30% charge remaining, and the packs Tejomay pulled for inspection at 700 cycles measured 91% state of health. Nobody questioned 1,800.

In 2024 Tejomay signed its first two fleet contracts, and the mix changed. Fleet riders swapped more often and, crucially, differently — they topped up. A gig rider between orders would swap at 45% rather than ride to 15%, because a full pack meant no interruption during a surge window. Revenue per swap stayed the same. Energy delivered per swap fell by roughly a third. The swap counter, which was the metric on every dashboard in the company and in every investor update, no longer meant what it had meant in 2023.

In early 2025 Aniruddh Deshmukh's battery team in Pune began seeing packs from Delhi and Hyderabad reaching 85% state of health at around 800 cycles, well ahead of the curve. Aniruddh attributed it to ambient heat and to the fast-charge profile Tejomay ran in cabinets to turn packs around quickly in the evening peak. He proposed derating the charge rate above 38 °C. Operations objected: derating in summer would cut cabinet throughput at exactly the hours when demand peaked. A compromise was reached that nobody had modelled.

In November 2025, firmware 3.1 shipped. Among other changes, it replaced the state-of-health estimator: the old method inferred capacity from a coulomb count between fixed voltage points, the new one used an impedance-based model that Tanvi Raghunathan's team in Toronto had validated against forty teardown packs. The new method read, on average, 3 to 5 percentage points lower on the same pack. Nobody flagged that the company's degradation trend line now contained a step change that was measurement, not physics. The FY26 board decks showed an alarming acceleration in degradation from December onwards.

In March 2026 Nimisha Arora, the CFO, attempted to claim against the supplier warranty for 2,240 packs that had fallen below 80% before 1,800 cycles. The supplier accepted 268 of them. The rest were rejected for insufficient evidence: the warranty required per-cycle temperature and charge-rate logs at a resolution Tejomay's cabinets had only begun capturing after firmware 3.1, and the claim period for the older packs had partly lapsed.

And in June 2026, Charmaine's Dubai pilot produced the most uncomfortable data of all — packs in 45 °C ambient degrading at roughly twice the Bengaluru rate. Barq wanted to expand to 2,000 scooters. Charmaine wanted the expansion. The degradation numbers had been in an annexe of her monthly report since July.

5. The people

Kartik Bhandari, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Owns the recommendation. Believes the company's core metric — swaps — has quietly stopped measuring anything real, but has not yet found a replacement he can defend in front of directors who have been shown swap growth for four years.

Sunaina Kamath, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Position: sign Pratidin. Incentive: a Series C conversation opens in January and density is the story that raises it; she also chose NMC in 2022 and has defended the choice publicly at three conferences. Not saying: that she has already indicated to two directors, informally, that the deal is winnable at ₹58.

Aniruddh Deshmukh, Head of Battery Engineering, Pune. Position: do not sign at ₹58 without a depth-of-discharge and temperature clause. Incentive: his team is judged on pack longevity, which fleet duty cycles destroy. Not saying: his own 2024 derating proposal was partly rejected because he could not quantify the throughput cost, and he has never gone back to quantify it.

Nimisha Arora, CFO, Bengaluru. Position: the replacement reserve must rise before any new contract is priced. Incentive: the auditors have already asked about the reserve, and the failed warranty claim is a visible embarrassment. Not saying: the current reserve was set using the supplier's 1,800 cycles precisely because a lower number would have made the FY25 accounts difficult.

Tanvi Raghunathan, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the degradation series is not comparable across November 2025 and should be restated before any decision. Incentive: her impedance model is her team's flagship and she does not want it blamed for a scare. Not saying: she raised the comparability issue in a design document in October 2025 that three people read, and she has not raised it since in a forum where it would have been minuted.

Harmeet Singh Sethi, Regional Operations Head, Delhi NCR. Position: sign, at almost any price. Incentive: his stations run at 21% utilisation and his cost base is fixed rent; his quarterly bonus is tied to station contribution. Not saying: about 14% of the packs assigned to his region have not been seen by a cabinet in over sixty days and are presumed held by riders or lost, and his utilisation denominator excludes them.

Lukas Behrend, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the app should discourage top-up swaps above 40% with a price nudge, which would raise energy per swap and slow degradation. Incentive: he has been pushing a redesign for two quarters. Not saying: his own user research showed fleet riders would simply queue at the cabinet and wait, which would worsen peak congestion.

Charmaine Koh, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: expand the Dubai pilot to 2,000 scooters this quarter. Incentive: international expansion is her mandate and the pilot is her only reference account. Not saying: how far the Gulf degradation data diverges from the India curve, and that Barq has asked for a pack-replacement guarantee she has not yet priced.

Dev Mathur, Head of Sales, New Jersey. Position: publish a cycle-life figure the datasheet can carry. Incentive: two US licensing deals stall without one. Not saying: he has already quoted 1,800 cycles in writing to one prospect.

7. Voices

Sunaina Kamath, CEO — leadership meeting, 14 September

"We are arguing about the third decimal of a degradation curve while a competitor signs 41 lakh swaps. Density is the moat. Get me to yes on Pratidin and we will fix the battery maths with a bigger balance sheet."

Aniruddh Deshmukh, Pune — reply on the same thread, 06:12 the next morning

"With respect: at Pratidin's duty cycle we will be buying the packs twice inside the contract term. I am not against the deal. I am against signing a three-year price against a cost we have not measured once."

Tanvi Raghunathan, Toronto — chat to Kartik, 11 September, 23:40 IST

"Before you put Exhibit 2 in a board pack — the two halves of that line are different instruments. I wrote this up last October. I can restate the series but I need four weeks and two engineers, and I'd rather the board heard it from us than from a diligence team in January."

Harmeet Singh Sethi, Delhi NCR — operations review, 9 September

"Sir, in Delhi we do not have a demand problem, we have an empty-cabinet problem. Give me the Pratidin volume and my stations turn positive in one quarter. Whatever the price is."

Nimisha Arora, CFO — note to the audit committee, 3 September

"The FY27 reserve range is ₹10 crore to ₹27 crore depending on the cycle-life basis adopted. I am not able to recommend a basis until product and engineering agree a single definition of pack retirement."

Lukas Behrend, Berlin — design review, 8 September

"Every top-up swap is revenue today and wear tomorrow. We built a product that is paid for the wrong unit. If we charged for energy the whole behaviour changes — and so does half of this argument."

Charmaine Koh, Singapore — weekly report annexe, 7 September

"Barq is ready for 2,000 units in Q3 subject to a replacement guarantee. Gulf ambient conditions remain a variable in our degradation observations; recommend engineering review before commercial commitment."

8. The options as Kartik sees them

He had written three on the whiteboard, and had been staring at them long enough to distrust the list itself.

One: sign at ₹58 with volume protection. Fill the network, take Delhi positive, buy the density that makes a Series C possible. Accept that the pack cost per swap is unknown and rely on scale and future chemistry improvements to close the gap. The exposure is that a three-year fixed price against a cost base that Exhibit 4 says might be ₹17 crore a year worse than booked is, in substance, a bet that the middle column of that exhibit is wrong.

Two: counter at ₹66 with a depth-of-discharge and temperature clause. Price the duty cycle explicitly — a lower rate for swaps arriving below 25% charge, a surcharge above 40%, and a summer derating protocol agreed in advance. Pratidin has never signed such a structure and may walk. Aniruddh supports it; Harmeet regards it as a way of losing the deal while sounding rigorous.

Three: decline, and spend the next four quarters on the asset. Restate the degradation series, renegotiate the supplier warranty with evidentiary terms Tejomay can actually meet, pilot a cabinet revision that accepts an LFP pack alongside NMC, and rebuild the commercial model around energy delivered. The cost is a year of flat growth entering a funding conversation, and the near-certainty that a competitor takes Pratidin's volume and the density that goes with it.

What unsettled him was a sentence Lukas had said in a design review and nobody had picked up: we built a product that is paid for the wrong unit. If revenue per kilowatt-hour rather than revenue per swap was the honest denominator, then Pratidin at ₹58 was not obviously a discount at all — Exhibit 3 suggested large fleets already paid the highest rate per kilowatt-hour on the network. In which case the argument in the room for three weeks had been about the wrong quantity, and the options on his whiteboard were three answers to a question he had not yet asked properly.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board met at 11 a.m. on Monday 21 September. Pratidin's tender closed on 30 September and the company had indicated it would not extend. Tejomay held ₹96 crore of cash against a monthly burn of ₹6.8 crore, giving about fourteen months of runway, and had ₹62 crore of FY27 capex approved, of which ₹41 crore was already committed to cabinet rollout in Hyderabad and Pune. The pack supplier's contract carried a minimum annual order quantity of 9,000 units, renewable in December, with a 90-day notice clause. Station leases in Delhi NCR ran to March 2028 with no early exit. The extended producer responsibility obligation meant that every pack retired had to be routed to a registered recycler with documentation, at a cost of roughly ₹1,100 a pack that appeared nowhere in Exhibit 1. Tanvi's restatement of the degradation series, if commissioned, would take four weeks and two engineers who were currently building the cabinet telemetry that Dev's American licensing deals required.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What does Tejomay currently believe a pack is worth over its life, and how many different answers to that question can you find in the exhibits? Which inputs in Exhibit 1 are measurements and which are assumptions?

2. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 4 both depend on the state-of-health estimator. What would you need to know before you allowed either to inform a three-year price, and what would you do if you could not know it by Monday?

3. Exhibit 3 shows large fleets paying less per swap and more per kilowatt-hour. Which denominator should govern Tejomay's pricing, and what does your answer imply about the swap counter that appears in every investor update?

4. Harmeet's utilisation figure excludes packs unseen for thirty days; Exhibit 6 stops before pack cost. If you corrected both, how would the Delhi case change — and what does that tell you about where the company's fleet metrics have been optimised for whom?

5. Several stakeholders are holding something back: Tanvi's October design document, Charmaine's Gulf annexe, Harmeet's missing packs, Nimisha's reason for the current reserve basis. What does each omission cost the company, and what mechanism would have surfaced them earlier?

6. What should Kartik do on Monday morning, and what exactly should he say to the board — about the Pratidin price, about the reserve, and about the number the company has been reporting as growth for four years?

11. Quarter past eleven

The test rig in the corner completed another swap cycle and clicked. Kartik pulled up slide 11 again. He had, in the last hour, drafted three different versions of the recommendation line and deleted all of them. The first said sign. The second said counter. The third said something longer about denominators that he knew would not survive the first question from a director who had been shown swap growth since 2022 and had never been told that a swap in 2026 carried two-thirds of the energy of a swap in 2023.

Somewhere in Toronto it was mid-afternoon, and Tanvi was probably still at her desk. In Pune, Aniruddh had sent a one-line message an hour ago — call me before you send it — and had not gone to sleep. In Delhi, Harmeet's cabinets stood two-thirds empty under the sodium lights of a fuel forecourt on the Noida road, waiting for a volume that Kartik could deliver by typing one number into one cell, and that he was no longer sure the company could afford to serve.

He looked at the placeholder on slide 11, and at the clock, and did not type anything.

Fleet and Device-Lifetime Metrics: The Deep Treatment

A device earns over a life it does not choose, on a clock nobody agrees about, measured with data that is systematically incomplete. This is the arithmetic, and the arguments.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 14 April 2026, Ananya Raghunathan, head of product at Gaurika Medical Systems in Bengaluru, took a one-page memo into a meeting she had asked for. Gaurika places connected oxygen concentrators with mid-sized hospitals and home-care aggregators on a device-as-a-service contract: ₹3,400 per unit per month, remote monitoring, and a service guarantee in the uptime language NABH-accredited hospitals expect. The model built for its Series B assumed each of its 4,200 fielded units would run sixty months, making a concentrator worth 2.4 times the ₹46,000 it cost to build, certify, ship and commission.

Ananya's memo said the number was not wrong so much as unanswerable in the form asked. Gaurika's oldest cohort was 29 months old; no unit had reached sixty. Pritam Saikia, the reliability engineer, computed average device life as the mean age of units that had failed — a figure that had climbed every quarter from 14 months to 22, which the executive team read as the product improving. It was an artefact of a fleet too young to have produced old failures. Ananya wanted a narrower question answered before the board met: given what Gaurika could actually observe, what was a concentrator worth over its life, and how confident could anyone be?

Six weeks later, on 26 May 2026, Kabir Jaitley met a different version of the problem at Indravati Energy Networks in Hyderabad. Indravati ran a battery-swapping network for gig-economy two-wheelers: 62,000 lithium packs cycling through 940 stations, riders paying per swap, hosts taking a share. Its dashboard had one hero number, swaps per pack per day, which the growth team had moved from 1.3 to 2.1 in nine months. After a fortnight with Dr. Ipshita Roy, Indravati's cell chemist, Kabir had reached a conclusion he did not want: the improvement had almost no effect on what a pack earned across its life. Packs wear out in cycles, not months, and the growth team had been optimising the rate at which Indravati spent a fixed budget.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A fleet and device-lifetime metric is any measure that describes a population of deployed physical units as a cohort moving through time, with an economic quantity attached to every state a unit can occupy: shipped but not activated, connected and earning, failed, removed, silent, recovered, refurbished, redeployed, written off. Its central claim is that hardware revenue and hardware cost are both integrals over a survival curve, not products of a headcount and a price.

The intellectual history merges three traditions with no prior reason to speak. From reliability engineering — Waloddi Weibull's 1951 paper on a distribution flexible enough to describe both infant mortality and wear-out — came hazard functions, censored data, and the recognition that a failure rate has a shape, not merely a level. From biostatistics came the tools for estimating survival when observation stops before the subject does: Kaplan–Meier, 1958, and later competing-risks methods. The problem the merger solves is specific: a device stops earning for physically, contractually and economically distinct reasons, and a business that cannot separate them cannot tell whether it has an engineering, a pricing or a logistics problem.

Four schools contest what the resulting metric should be. The reliability school makes the device the unit of analysis; it signs that failure shape by vintage and duty cycle is the primary driver of lifetime value, and refuses to sign that a unit switched off by a customer belongs on the same curve as one whose compressor seized. The cohort-finance school makes discounted cash the unit; it signs that all causes of revenue stoppage are economically identical at the moment they stop revenue, and refuses separate headline metrics for failure and churn. The asset-management school (from rental fleets and aviation) holds field life to be a managed rather than an observed variable; it signs that recovery, refurbishment and residual value sit inside the lifetime metric, and refuses to sign that a device which stops transmitting is lost. The account school makes the customer account the unit and devices seats; it signs that device attrition without account attrition is a fulfilment problem, and refuses per-device survival a board metric at all.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic experts actually run

A fleet holds units of many ages, most of which have not failed. A unit deployed nine months ago and still running tells you its life is at least nine months. That observation is right-censored, and the commonest error in hardware analytics — Pritam's error — is to average only the uncensored ones, an estimator biased downward in level and upward in trend, which is why it rises every quarter and looks like progress.

The non-parametric correction is the Kaplan–Meier estimator: at each month t with failures, take the conditional survival 1 − dt/nt, where nt counts units still under observation at the start of that month, so censored units leave the denominator without counting as failures; the running product is S(t). It assumes no shape, and says nothing about months the fleet has not yet lived — the region a board asks about. Hence the parametric layer: the Weibull, S(t) = exp(−(t/η)β), with mean life η·Γ(1 + 1/β). The shape β is what matters. Below one the hazard falls with age — infant mortality, the signature of commissioning defects. At one it is constant, the distribution memoryless. Above one damage accumulates and the hazard rises.

Expected discounted device margin = Σt S(t)·m·vt  −  Σt f(t)·(W − R)·vt  −  C0

Here m is contribution per connected device-month, v = 1/(1+r) the monthly discount factor, f(t) the failure density, W the cost of servicing a failure, R expected recovered value, and C0 the fully loaded cost of deployment. Re-fitted with censoring handled properly, Gaurika's data gave β = 2.3 and η = 41 months — wear-out, consistent with sieve-bed and compressor degradation — a mean life of 36.3 months, not sixty. Contribution was ₹2,050 a month net of connectivity, consumables and service; the discount rate 1.1% monthly; W ₹9,800; the chassis worth ₹4,100, but only 43% of failed units came back, so realised recovery was ₹1,763.

The second-order effect: shape dominates level

Hold mean life at 36 months and change only the shape. An exponential fleet — β = 1, η = 36, same mean — loses 28% of its units in the first year, when each surviving month is worth most. The identical arithmetic gives 23.4 discounted device-months, ₹48,011 of contribution, and a net position of negative ₹3,168.

Figure 1. Survival against fleet age for two fitted curves with identical mean life. The shaded area is what earns; the dashed curve gives its area away early, when discounting penalises the loss least.

The managerial reading is blunt: mean time between failures cannot determine whether a fleet makes money, since two products with identical MTBF can sit on opposite sides of breakeven. β is a design parameter, not a statistic, and the decisions that set it — burn-in, commissioning checklists, whether a consumable is field-replaceable — are lifetime-value decisions taken without anyone computing their effect.

Competing risks, and the choice of clock

The arithmetic above assumed that "stops earning" means "failed". Units leave by several routes at once, and the correct formalism is competing risks: cause-specific hazards for hardware failure, contract termination and unexplained silence, yielding cumulative incidence functions that sum with survival to one. The practical yield is a decomposition, at any fleet age, of where the population has gone.

Figure 2. Cumulative incidence for one ship-month cohort. The three exits cost differently: a failure consumes a visit and a part, a termination returns an asset, a dark unit returns nothing.

Dr. Roy's contribution was to observe that the same formalism needs a different clock: cells degrade with charge throughput and thermal stress, so the natural axis is equivalent full cycles. A pack rated at 1,400 cycles to 80% state of health under 1C laboratory charging delivers roughly 980 under the 1.6C fast-swap duty Indravati's stations run. At 2.1 swaps a day — 63 a month — that budget is spent in 15.6 months. At the suburban clusters' 0.9 a day it lasts far longer, but calendar ageing binds first at about 36 months. The regimes converge on almost the same lifetime cycles, which Kabir had not expected.

4. When the framework applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions govern whether lifetime fleet metrics should drive decisions. First: economic output is spread over time rather than realised at sale. Where a device is sold outright with no service revenue and no warranty tail, the lifetime view adds little to a gross-margin line. Gaurika passes emphatically, earning nothing at shipment and everything afterwards; Indravati passes strangely, since its output is spread over usage rather than time, so the metric must be rebuilt on the usage axis or it misleads systematically.

Second: exit from the earning population is materially probabilistic and only partly observable. If units essentially never fail and never go dark, survival modelling is ceremony. Gaurika passes — 11.8% of a cohort has confirmed-failed by month 24, with a further 3.6% dark. Indravati fails on hardware terms and passes on others: packs rarely vanish, but state of health is partially observable, drifts, and is contested between operations and finance.

Third: the marginal cost of a lost unit is large relative to its monthly contribution. A ₹46,000 concentrator against ₹2,050 a month passes overwhelmingly; a ₹400 sensor against ₹300 a month would not, and there the apparatus collapses into a cost line.

The framework is actively misleading in three situations. When new deployments dominate the base, any fleet-wide ratio improves during a heavy shipping quarter purely by dilution while every cohort deteriorates. When useful life is ended by obsolescence rather than failure, survival curves answer the wrong question precisely. And when the device is not the economic unit — a hospital buys oxygen availability across a ward, which Gaurika could satisfy with fewer machines — optimising per-device lifetime value deploys more assets than the customer needs.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Regulation changes what the metric is permitted to say. Gaurika's concentrators are notified devices under the CDSCO framework, so a confirmed field failure is not merely a cost event but a record in a complaints file with reporting obligations. That creates an incentive nobody writes down: calling an ambiguous unit "dark, cause unknown" is cheaper than calling it failed, on both the warranty reserve and the regulatory file. Ananya found the dark rate rising for three consecutive quarters while confirmed failures stayed flat — in her judgement classification drift at the service-desk seam, not physics.

Two-sided structures put the device and the revenue on different sides. Indravati's packs sit in stations owned by hosts and are used by riders whose loyalty is to price, so pack survival depends on a host's electrical quality and a rider's charging discipline, neither of which Indravati controls. The metric must be cut by host and rider segment or it aggregates away the only available levers.

Hardware-plus-software fleets raise the obsolescence seam. A firmware release can extend useful life, or end it by demanding memory the installed generation lacks. At Hemadri Controls, a Pune maker of industrial edge controllers, a platform decision to move to a container runtime stranded 9,000 first-generation units that were physically healthy and contractually earning. That cohort's survival curve has a vertical cliff at the release date — an accurate description of an event no reliability model could predict, because the hazard was written in a sprint plan.

AI-native fleets add a reflexive twist. When telemetry feeds a predictive-maintenance model that triggers pre-emptive replacement, the observed hazard falls because the metric acted on it, and the curve becomes a joint product of hardware and policy. Mature teams hold out a control slice, three to five per cent of the fleet, so the underlying hazard stays observable. Most companies say they do this. Rather fewer sustain it past the first quarter in which the control slice produces a visible, attributable outage.

The deepest seam is accounting. Whether a device-as-a-service contract is a lease under Ind AS 116 or a service arrangement determines whether the device sits on the balance sheet and what "payback" means. Gaurika's finance team computed payback against a depreciated carrying value; Ananya's team against cash deployed. The two differed by 40%, and neither team had known the other existed.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Censoring is the default state. The tell is a mean-device-life figure that improves every quarter in a growing fleet. The obvious reading — reliability is improving — is wrong: the estimator averages a biased sample, the units that failed early. An expert asks for the survival curve and the number at risk each month before any average, and treats a lifetime figure with no censoring convention as uninterpretable.

Shape governs value more than level does. The tell is a warranty reserve driven by a single MTBF. The obvious reading is that mean life summarises reliability adequately; it does not, because discounting weights early months most and the same mean distributes very differently across them. An expert treats infant mortality and wear-out as different businesses with different remedies.

Exits compete, and the competition is informative. The tell is a single attrition line combining failures, cancellations and silences. The obvious reading is that all three stop revenue and belong together — true for the cash forecast, false for every operating decision, because reliability, pricing and field logistics are different budgets with different owners. An expert keeps the decomposition at every fleet age and reconciles it to the cash number.

The clock is a choice, and the default is usually wrong. The tell is a fleet whose annualised failure rate varies three-fold across regions with no plausible quality explanation. The obvious reading is environmental variation. Often the device ages on another axis entirely — cycles, run hours, print volume, thermal load — for which calendar months are a noisy proxy. An expert establishes the wear axis empirically before fitting anything to it.

Dark is a third state with an asymmetric cost of error. The tell is that nobody can quote the reconnection rate of units dark for thirty days. The obvious reading is that dark units are dead and should be written off — conservative on revenue, reckless on assets, since such a unit may be recoverable inventory, a coverage gap, or a customer quietly using it offline. An expert measures the reconnection distribution and prices both errors separately.

Utilisation is not free when the asset is consumption-limited. The tell is an operations incentive on throughput sitting beside straight-line depreciation in the same statement. The obvious reading is that more usage is more revenue; where life is measured in cycles, extra usage also pulls replacement capital forward, and total lifetime earnings may be nearly invariant to it, as Indravati found. An expert states whether a throughput programme buys timing or earnings.

Reverse logistics belongs inside the metric. The tell is a model assuming recovery of failed units at a rate nobody measures. The obvious reading is that recovery is an operations detail; it is frequently the difference between a positive and a negative unit economic, as Gaurika's 43% return rate was. An expert owns the return rate and treats residual value as a forecast with an error bar.

Definitions drift under incentive pressure. The tell is a category whose share grows steadily while its neighbours stay flat — Gaurika's rising dark rate against a static failure rate. The obvious reading is a real shift in field conditions; frequently it is a classification boundary moving, because one label costs the organisation more than another. An expert re-adjudicates a random sample blind to the original label, and expects to find drift.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer hardware the fragile stage is activation and the dominant exit is silent. Haveli Home Systems, which rents connected water purifiers to households, loses more units to families moving house than to component failure, and its curve carries a seasonal sawtooth tracking urban rental cycles. In B2B and enterprise fleets the install is professional, activation approaches unity, and the variance moves to the contract: a service-level agreement converts downtime into a priced liability, so the same failure costs differently depending which clause it trips. On platforms and marketplaces the device belongs to one party and earns from another, making recovery rather than reliability the binding constraint. In AI-native products useful life is increasingly set by whether the unit can run the current model, so the hazard acquires a term that lives in the roadmap.

Where the differences are not real is worth saying plainly. The survival arithmetic is identical in all these settings. Censoring bias, competing risks, discounting and cohort dilution behave exactly the same for a purifier, a concentrator, a battery pack and a payment terminal. What changes is the clock, the exit mix, and who bears the cost of each exit — not the mathematics.

Stage changes the failure mode rather than the method. A seed-stage company with 300 units can manage by inspecting a list; fitting nine months of history yields intervals wide enough to justify any decision, so what matters is instrumenting the exit states so the data exists later. Between roughly 2,000 and 20,000 units the practice must formalise, because fleet-wide intuition stops working and dilution flatters every aggregate. Past that the constraint is organisational: the metric spans product, reliability, field service, finance and, in regulated categories, quality assurance, and its integrity depends on one person owning the definition across all five.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Gaurika, and the value of getting the shape right. Having established β = 2.3, Ananya's team asked what would move the number most. A larger sieve bed, adding ₹3,100 to unit cost, shifted η from 41 to 52 months, lifting discounted device-months from 28.3 to 33.6 and contribution to ₹68,880; net of the extra cost and a lighter failure load, expected margin per unit rose from ₹6,921 to about ₹16,400. The same ₹3,100 spent on remote diagnostics would have improved first-visit fix rates and saved perhaps ₹900 a unit. The comparison was possible only because both had been translated into one currency: discounted device-months.

Indravati, and the price that was never operations' fault. Kabir ran the arithmetic backwards. A lithium-iron-phosphate pack at ₹38,000 delivers roughly 2,200 cycles under swap duty — 35 months at urban utilisation — with a second-life value of ₹9,200; discounted, that is ₹17,120 of contribution and ₹6,274 of residual against a ₹38,000 asset, still ₹14,600 short. Solving for the contribution that closes the gap gave ₹17.41 per swap against the ₹9.40 Indravati earned — an 85% increase. No operational programme closes an 85% gap. The chemistry change was necessary and insufficient; the honest conclusion was that the owned-asset model required a different price or a different owner of the asset.

Ishira Metering, and the denominator that hid the problem. Ishira, an advanced-metering service provider on a discom contract under the national distribution reform programme, had the most admired dashboard of the three. Its headline metric, communication success rate, ran at 98.4% for eleven months. In early 2026 Nandini Vaze, the programme director, found it was computed only over meters that had reached commissioned status; roughly 11% of those the discom had handed over sat in a pending-site-readiness state, some for fourteen months, excluded from the denominator entirely. On the contractually relevant base — meters received — the figure was 87.6%. The denominator had been chosen by an analytics team to describe a system it could control, then read by a board as describing the programme. Recovery took seven months, cost about ₹3.2 crore in deferred milestone revenue, and was organisational: every metric was re-based on meters received, ownership moved to the delivery head, and weekly reconciliation against the discom's asset register became a standing item. Nandini's summary was that the dashboard had been honest about the wrong population, which is harder to catch than a dishonest dashboard about the right one.

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of catching them late

Denominator laundering. Early sign: a metric whose base is defined by a state the reporting team controls. Diagnostic question: which units are excluded, and who decided? Caught late it costs a renegotiation — Ishira's ₹3.2 crore — because commitments were made on the flattered number.

Throughput incentives on consumption-limited assets. Early sign: operations compensated on utilisation while finance depreciates on calendar. Diagnostic question: is a marginal unit of usage accretive after replacement capital expenditure? Caught late, the fleet needs an unbudgeted replacement wave, usually in the quarter after a successful growth push.

The unowned metric. Early sign: fleet health is assembled for board meetings rather than reviewed on a cadence. Diagnostic question: who reads the cohort curves weekly, and what decision changes if they move? Caught late, the cost is months of undetected drift — Gaurika's classification shift ran three quarters.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should dark units count as lost? The conservative position, held by most finance functions, is that an asset which cannot be observed should be assumed gone, resting on the observation that reconnection rates after ninety days are low in most fleets. The asset-management position is that write-off destroys the recovery incentive: once a unit leaves the books, nobody funds the visit to retrieve it, and the assumption becomes self-fulfilling; it rests on rental-fleet evidence that recovery responds sharply to whether recovery is anyone's target. The conservative view is wrong if retrieval rates prove responsive to effort; the asset-management view is wrong if they prove stubbornly low regardless. Both camps cite fleets; neither has published a study the other accepts.

Device or account as the unit of analysis? The device school argues that only per-device survival exposes physics and batch effects, and that account-level metrics mask reliability problems inside large customers who tolerate failures rather than churn. The account school argues that devices are fungible within an account, that a customer who replaces a failed unit and stays has cost only a service call, and that device-churn metrics generate roadmap work on problems already forgiven. The device school is wrong where the contract buys an outcome rather than a unit; the account school is wrong wherever devices are separately priced.

Parametric or non-parametric, and discounted or not? Fitting a Weibull to 29 months and extrapolating to sixty imports an assumption the data cannot test; Kaplan–Meier refuses to extrapolate and so refuses to answer the board's question. Alongside sits an older quarrel: cohort-finance practitioners insist on discounting device margin at the cost of capital, while a minority of industrial practitioners argue that monthly discounting biases against long-lived assets in ways that have hollowed out durability as a design goal, preferring undiscounted payback with a life cap. The first is right about capital and can be wrong about products; the second is right about products and evades what the money could otherwise do. Which to adopt depends on whether the decision is reversible — a judgement, not a statistic.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves in identifiable ways. Shown a lifetime number, they ask for the clock before the value — months, cycles, run hours, throughput — because the axis determines what follows. They ask what fraction of observations are censored, and can tell within a minute whether a figure was computed over survivors. They refuse point-in-time connected percentages without a cohort cut beside them. They translate every engineering investment into discounted device-months, which makes a sieve bed and a diagnostics module comparable. They know their return rate and who owns it, and treat the boundary between failed and dark as an organisational artefact to be audited rather than a fact to be read. And when told a fleet metric has improved, their first question is whether the fleet got better or simply got younger.

12. What each protagonist decided

Ananya Raghunathan went to the Gaurika board on 5 June 2026 with three recommendations and one retraction. The retraction was the sixty-month life assumption, replaced by a fitted 36-month mean with a stated confidence band. The recommendations were to fund the larger sieve bed, on the strength of the ₹9,500-per-unit swing in discounted margin; to give the dark-unit rate a named owner in field service, with monthly blind re-adjudication of a sample; and to stop reporting MTBF to the board, replacing it with the cohort survival curve and the discounted-device-month figure. Her reasoning was that the company had been managing a number incapable of distinguishing two products worth ₹10,000 apart per unit.

Kabir Jaitley's decision was harder, because the arithmetic pointed at the business model rather than the roadmap. He recommended retiring swaps per pack per day in favour of contribution per cycle, and opening negotiations with the three largest fleet-operator customers on a per-swap price the pack could support. He also recommended piloting an arrangement in which large operators own the packs and Indravati operates the network — asset-light, trading margin for removal of the cycle-budget problem from the balance sheet. The pricing committee approved the metric change immediately and the pilot with visible reluctance.

Three questions for discussion. If Gaurika's β had come back at 0.8 rather than 2.3 — infant mortality rather than wear-out — which of Ananya's recommendations would you reverse, and what would you propose instead? Indravati's growth team delivered exactly what it was asked for and moved a metric that turned out not to matter: where should responsibility sit, and what would have caught it in month two rather than month nine? And Ishira's dashboard was accurate about the population it described — what general rule would have caused someone to challenge its denominator before a board committed to milestones built on it?

13. Going deeper

Hardware and connected-product metrics is the parent frame, setting out the instrumentation surface from which lifetime measures are drawn. Device telemetry and fleet analytics supplies the raw material: without a disciplined event model for heartbeat, fault and state transitions, the decomposition in Figure 2 cannot be built. What makes a good metric is the sharpest test to apply here — a fleet number with no owner, cadence or attached decision fails it whatever its sophistication. Vanity versus actionable metrics is Indravati's lesson generalised: swaps per pack per day was neither, but a real operational measure attached to the wrong economic claim. The GAME framework helps decide which fleet measure belongs in a goal tree rather than a diagnostic panel. Acquisition, retention and monetisation actions maps the exits of Figure 2 onto the interventions that address each, which is how a decomposition becomes a roadmap. Direct versus proxy, magnitude versus ratio explains why connected percentage misleads during growth while connected device-months does not. And North Star metric is where section 10's unresolved question belongs: whether a fleet business can have a single north star at all, or whether device-lifetime economics are irreducibly a vector read together.
